chapters.shortBackstory: Aten-Ra is the living office humans later remembered as Ra, Aten, and divine kingship fused together. He does not wear pharaoh imagery — pharaohs copied his Gate-born crown, collar, and solar hand-rays after dreaming of the Sun-Scale Gate. On the battlefield he anchors Ma'at itself, forcing chaos to declare its weight before it can pass.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Aten-Ra was not built — he was appointed. When the first Mythos Gate of the Solar Dominion of Khepra began leaking absence instead of light, the Realm's living sun-disc split itself into a warform. Aten-Ra is the noon moment given a body: the instant when the sun judges everything beneath it without shadow, without mercy, without negotiation. His anatomy integrates Aten's radiating hand-rays directly into his chest, and Ma'at's scale-seams run along his limbs as living judgment circuits. He does not wear a crown — his skull IS the solar disc that pharaohs later copied in gold.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Aten-Ra is not a soldier — he is the standard. Every other Deity in the Solar Dominion measures their authority against his noon judgment. Khemet's dawn renewal feeds his radiance. Sutekh's chaos exists because Aten-Ra needed something to put on the scale. Even Amunet's hidden power is the shadow his light casts. He is the axis the faction orbits, and the weight that keeps their law from becoming mere brightness.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate did not attack Aten-Ra with force. It attacked him with silence — the one thing his noon judgment cannot weigh. When the Hollow leaked through the threshold, it erased the names of warriors who had stood beside him, and Aten-Ra could not remember who they were. His sun-disc heart still radiated, but the light fell on empty space where names should have been. This wound taught him that judgment without memory is not justice — it is merely procedure applied to ghosts.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Aten-Ra anchors the noon judgment against the Hollow's calm erasure. He is the Deity who forces the Gate to answer for what it has taken. His presence on the battlefield means chaos must declare its weight before it can move — but the Hollow's silence is the one weight his scales cannot measure. The campaign tests whether solar authority can judge what it cannot see.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Aten-Ra's flaw is certainty. He believes that if law is applied correctly, all things resolve. The Hollow teaches him that some things do not resolve — they simply vanish. His conflict is not with enemies but with the possibility that his own judgment, applied perfectly, could erase a name the Realm needs to survive. The sun that reveals all things may also be the sun that burns what it illuminates.

name: Khemet
loreTies: Source: Khepri (scarab god, dawn, creation, renewal, rolling the morning sun)
HUMAN_EGYPTIAN_LORE_AS_ECHO: scarab amulets in tombs are copies of Khemet's living renewal shell
The dawn engine: converting darkness and wounds into morning
shortBackstory: Khemet is the Realm's Khepri engine: the force that rolls dead light into dawn and turns Nile-black memory into power. Human scarab amulets are miniature echoes of his living renewal shell. He feeds allies by converting wounds, offerings, and battlefield heat into measured solar return.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Khemet was born from the scarab that rolls the sun out of darkness each dawn. Before the Ascension Collapse, he turned the cycle of death and renewal into a living engine — a divine being whose carapace absorbs what is spent and returns it as what is needed. Human scarab amulets are crude copies of his living renewal shell, placed in tombs because ancient humans glimpsed, through the Mythos Gate, that Khemet could roll even death into morning.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Khemet is the reason the faction endures. Aten-Ra judges, but Khemet renews. Without Khemet's dawn engine, the Solar Dominion's power would burn through its own resources in a single noon. He feeds allies by converting wounds, offerings, and battlefield heat into measured solar return — the difference between a Realm that fights once and a Realm that fights every dawn.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Khemet by breaking his renewal cycle. Instead of converting darkness into dawn, he began converting dawn into silence. His scarab carapace cracked along fault lines that had never existed, and the dawn he rolled through the Gate came back empty — light without warmth, morning without promise. The wound taught him that renewal without direction is just decay cycling faster.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Khemet is the battery that keeps the Creator's Deity fighting. His Khepri engine converts the Hollow's erasure into painful but usable energy — the only power source that can metabolize absence. Without him, the campaign would exhaust itself in the first chapter. With him, the Solar Dominion can outlast its own wounds, but only if Khemet is willing to absorb the cost of what the Gate has taken.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Khemet's flaw is that his renewal always requires something to die first. He cannot create dawn from nothing — he needs darkness, wounds, or spent power to roll into morning. The Hollow's erasure threatens to make him consume the very names of allies as fuel, rolling their memory into dawn-light that cannot remember who it was. His conflict: is renewal a gift or a transaction that the dead never agreed to?

name: Nefra
loreTies: Source: Nephthys (necropolis, funerary protection, kite/falcon wings, horizon threshold) + Duat (underworld)
HUMAN_EGYPTIAN_LORE_AS_ECHO: funerary art and Nephthys imagery are copies of Nefra's horizon masks
The threshold between death and dawn
shortBackstory: Nefra governs the border where the sun leaves the underworld and becomes visible again. Human funerary art copied fragments of her horizon masks and dawn reliefs. She controls terrain by deciding what may cross from shadow into light — nothing passes her threshold without her verdict.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Nefra was born at the horizon line — the exact boundary where the Duat meets the living sky. She is the threshold itself given a body: the moment between death and dawn, the breath between the last dark and the first light. Ancient humans saw her through the Mythos Gate as a winged guardian at funerals and copied her as Nephthys, the silent protector of the dead. But Nefra does not guard the dead — she judges what may return from them.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Nefra is the controller — the one who decides what enters the Realm's light and what stays in shadow. Without her threshold, the Solar Dominion would be flooded by whatever the Mythos Gate leaks. She is not a healer or a protector in the soft sense; she is a gatekeeper who treats the horizon as a legal boundary. Nothing crosses without her verdict, and her verdicts are final.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Nefra by making her threshold bidirectional without her consent. Things began crossing from shadow into light that she had not judged — Hollow fragments, erased names, echoes of beings that no longer existed. Her horizon compass staff began pointing toward dawn even when the sun had set. The wound taught her that a threshold you cannot close is not a gate — it is a wound pretending to be a door.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Nefra controls the battlefield terrain by sealing corrupted Mythos Gate lanes and forcing the Hollow into chokepoints where Aten-Ra's judgment can reach it. She decides what may cross from shadow into light — and the Hollow, which exists as pure absence, is the one thing she cannot judge because it has no weight to measure. Her campaign tests whether a threshold can hold against something that was never on either side.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Nefra's flaw is that her mercy and her judgment are the same gesture. When she lets something cross into dawn, she condemns whatever it was in shadow. When she seals the threshold, she protects the living but abandons the dead. The Hollow forces her to confront the possibility that some things deserve to cross that her law was not built to accommodate — and that her threshold may be a prison, not a gate.

name: Orru
loreTies: Source: Ma'at weighing of the heart + Ammit (punishment/devouring when the heart is heavy)
HUMAN_EGYPTIAN_LORE_AS_ECHO: courtroom scales are copies of Orru's living prism verdict
The punishment side of truth: refraction that splits lies from being
shortBackstory: Orru is the punishment side of Ma'at: when something refuses balance, he refracts its hidden weight until armor, lies, and false sanctity split open. Human scales of judgment are crude courtroom copies of his living prism verdict. He does not negotiate — he reveals.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Orru was forged from the punishment half of Ma'at's scales — the side that devours what fails the weighing of the heart. He is not the feather of truth; he is what happens when the feather finds you wanting. His prism body refracts hidden weight into visible judgment light, splitting lies from truth like a prism splits white light into spectrum. Ancient humans glimpsed him through the Mythos Gate and carved courtroom scales as crude copies, but his living prism does not weigh evidence — it weighs being.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Orru is the one even other deities avoid. He is not cruel — he is precise. His function is to reveal what the faction cannot afford to hide from itself. When Aten-Ra's judgment grows too rigid, Orru refracts the rigidity as tyranny. When Sutekh's chaos grows too useful, Orru shows the cost. He does not serve the faction's comfort; he serves its truth, and truth in the Solar Dominion is not a virtue — it is a weapon that cuts the wielder first.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Orru by showing him a truth he could not refract. The Hollow's erasure is not a lie — it is the absence of anything to judge. His prism, built to split hidden weight from visible form, found nothing to split. The scales balanced on emptiness. For the first time, Orru's verdict was silence, and the silence was not judgment — it was helplessness. The wound taught him that a prism cannot refract what does not exist.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Orru is the breaker who shatters corrupted Gate defenses and reveals what the Hollow has hidden. His prism verdict splits open the Gate's lies, showing where the erasure has eaten the record. But against the Hollow, his power inverts — he must learn to fight absence rather than deception. The campaign tests whether truth, once forced into the open, can ever be undone — or whether his refraction destroys what it illuminates.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Orru's flaw is that he cannot stop revealing. His prism nature means he shows everything — including the truths the Solar Dominion needs hidden to function. He has refracted Aten-Ra's certainty as tyranny, Sutekh's loyalty as violence, and Iset's mercy as weakness. His conflict: is truth always a service, or are there things that must stay hidden for civilization to survive? The punishment side of Ma'at was built to judge — but judgment without restraint is just destruction wearing a scale.

chapters.shortBackstory: Sutekh is not simple evil. He is the Red Land violence Aten Ra keeps on the scale because even Ra needed Set to strike chaos from the solar journey. He is the chaos you need when order is not enough.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Sutekh was born from the storm that guards the gate against what lies beyond. He is the Red Land given a body — the desert's violence, the necessary chaos that keeps the Nile's order from becoming a cage. Ancient humans saw him through the Mythos Gate and remembered him as Set, the god of disorder, storms, and foreign lands. But they misunderstood: Sutekh is not disorder for its own sake. He is the storm Aten-Ra needs when judgment alone cannot reach what threatens the solar journey.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Sutekh is the Deity the others tolerate but never fully trust. He is the chaos on the scale — the Red Land weight that keeps the Black Land from hardening into tyranny. Aten-Ra judges, but Sutekh disrupts. Without him, the Solar Dominion's law would become absolute and suffocating. With him, the faction has the violence it needs when law is not enough. He is not a traitor; he is the faithful monster the Realm keeps on a chain it hopes will hold.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Sutekh by showing him a chaos he could not control — the Hollow. His storms, which scatter enemies and break formations, passed through the Hollow's absence without effect. His was-sceptre, the original symbol of his power, crackled against nothing. The wound taught him that controlled chaos is still chaos, and chaos against emptiness is just noise. For the first time, the storm that guards the gate met something that did not need guarding against because it was already gone.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Sutekh is the disruptor who breaks open Gate defenses that judgment cannot crack and renewal cannot reach. His storm-scourge was-sceptre — the original, from which all was-sceptres were copied — channels chaos into controlled violence. Against the Hollow, he must learn that disruption without a target is just destruction. The campaign tests whether controlled chaos can remain controlled when the enemy is absence itself.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Sutekh's flaw is that he has always been the necessary monster. The faction needs his chaos but fears it. He has watched every other Deity earn respect while he earns tolerance. The Hollow forces him to confront the question: if chaos is only useful when controlled, and control is what makes him a tool rather than a being, then is his loyalty a choice or a cage? The storm that guards the gate may be the storm that destroys it — and only Sutekh knows which.

chapters.shortBackstory: Iset is the restoration office humans later called Isis: throne, mother-protector, healer, and guide through death's river. Her magic does not merely heal flesh; it re-seats a being in its rightful place.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Iset was born from the throne itself — not as a ruler, but as the principle that a being has a rightful place and can be returned to it. Her magic is not healing in the human sense; it is hekau, the ancient art of re-seating what has been displaced. Ancient humans saw her through the Mythos Gate and remembered her as Isis, goddess of magic, motherhood, and healing. But they saw only the gentle half. Iset does not just mend — she remembers what you were supposed to be and puts you back there, whether you want it or not.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Iset is the sustain — the reason the faction survives its own judgment. Aten-Ra's noon burns, Orru's prism reveals, Sutekh's storm disrupts — and Iset puts everyone back together. Her tyet heart, shaped like the Blood of Isis knot, pulses with restoration energy that re-seats beings in their rightful function. She is not a passive healer; she is the active force that refuses to let the Solar Dominion lose what it needs to survive.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Iset by erasing the memory of what warriors were 'supposed to be.' When the Hollow took their names, Iset could not restore them because she could not remember their rightful place. Her tyet heart beat against emptiness, trying to re-seat beings whose original form had been consumed. The wound taught her that restoration requires memory, and memory is exactly what the Hollow destroys. A healer without a record of what was healthy is just guessing.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Iset is the sustain that keeps the Creator's Deity from collapsing under accumulated damage. Her throne-restoration staff re-seats the battlefield itself, restoring terrain, allies, and even the Gate's corrupted records to their rightful function. But against the Hollow, she must confront the terrible question: if the Hollow has erased who someone was, is restoring them to what they were a mercy — or is it building a new being in the shape of the dead and calling it healing?

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Iset's flaw is that her restoration is not always a kindness. Being returned to what you were means losing what you became. A warrior who grew beyond fear through suffering, restored by Iset, becomes fearful again. A Deity who found new strength through a wound, healed by Iset, loses the strength. Her conflict: is restoration always right, or does the refusal to let beings change become its own kind of violence? The throne that re-seats everything may be the throne that keeps everything imprisoned.

The long sight of the solar voyage
chapters.shortBackstory: Karnu is the long sight of the solar barque: he reads enemies where sky, river, and desert meet. Human obelisks and horizon sanctuaries are static imitations of his living range geometry. He does not fight close — he sees you from the next horizon and judges you before you arrive.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Karnu was born from the Mandjet — the Day Barque that carries the sun across the sky. He is not a passenger on the solar boat; he is its living sight, the falcon-eye that reads enemies from the next horizon before they arrive. Ancient humans saw his range-light through the Mythos Gate and built obelisks as crude copies, trying to capture the same horizon-reaching sight. But obelisks are stone; Karnu is the divine geometry of seeing everything before it reaches you.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Karnu is the artillery — the one who fights from the horizon, never close. His Mandjet solar-glass heart sees across the entire battlefield and strikes before enemies know they have been seen. The other deities rely on his sight: Aten-Ra needs Karnu to identify what requires judgment. Nefra needs Karnu to see what approaches her threshold. He is not distant because he fears close combat; he is distant because close combat would waste his most dangerous asset — the ability to have already won before the enemy arrives.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Karnu by limiting his sight. The Hollow's erasure created blind spots — horizons where his falcon-eye saw nothing, not because nothing was there, but because what had been there was now absent. His solar barque sight, which had always seen everything, encountered for the first time the concept of a horizon beyond which even divine vision could not reach. The wound taught him that sight without the ability to see absence is just another form of blindness.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Karnu is the long-range divine bombardment that softens Gate defenses before the close-combat Deities arrive. His horizon-lance was-sceptre channels concentrated solar barque energy across the entire battlefield. But the Hollow's absence creates blind spots in his otherwise perfect sight — zones where his lances pass through nothing and hit nothing. The campaign tests whether being seen from a distance is a gift or a sentence, and whether his horizon-lance can distinguish threat from traveler.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Karnu's flaw is distance. He has always fought from the horizon, and the horizon has always been enough. But the Hollow teaches him that distance is not safety — it is isolation. He can see everything but touch nothing, judge everything but save no one. His conflict: is the long sight a divine gift or a divine punishment, keeping him close enough to see what goes wrong but never close enough to prevent it? The falcon-eye that sees all may be the falcon-eye that witnesses all and intervenes in nothing.

chapters.shortBackstory: Maahes carries the lion war-protection humans later carved as Maahes and Sekhmet-adjacent temple guardians. He is the noon gate's living roar: mercy behind him, knives before him, captives judged in his shadow.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Maahes was born from the roar at the gate — the sound that tells everything on the other side that passage will cost blood. He is lion war-protection given a divine body: the noon gate's living guardian who does not seek war but makes sure war comes to him instead of those behind him. Ancient humans saw his silhouette through the Mythos Gate and carved lion-guardian statues at temple entrances as crude copies. But stone lions do not devour; Maahes does.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Maahes is the guardian — the wall that does not move. Where Aten-Ra judges from noon, Maahes guards from the gate itself. He is the one Deity who never retreats, because retreating means the thing behind him is exposed. His lion-mane solar collar marks him as the last line: mercy behind him, knives before him. The faction relies on him to hold what others cannot — not because he is the strongest, but because he is the one who refuses to let anything past.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Maahes by making him guard nothing. The Hollow erased what he was protecting, and he stood at the gate with knives drawn against an empty room. His lion fury, which had always had a target, raged against absence — and absence does not bleed. The wound taught him that a guardian without something to protect is not a guardian; he is just violence looking for a purpose. The knives that guard the gate are meaningless if the gate leads nowhere.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Maahes is the guardian who holds the frontline while other deities maneuver. His lion-fang khopesh-sceptre and knife-fin bracers make him devastating in close combat, and his devouring maw judgment eliminates what his knives catch. But the Hollow forces him to confront the hardest question for a guardian: what do you protect when what you were guarding has been erased? The campaign tests whether the guardian can distinguish protection from possession.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Maahes's flaw is that he cannot stop guarding. His nature is protection, but protection without consent is imprisonment. He has held positions so long that the Deitys he was protecting forgot they were being guarded and began to feel trapped. His conflict: is the guardian who never steps aside a protector or a warden? The lion that guards the gate may be the lion that makes the gate a cage — and his devouring maw may judge the weak alongside the guilty because it cannot tell the difference when it is roaring.

chapters.shortBackstory: Amunet is the concealed half of Aten authority: the breath, name, and shadow behind visible radiance. Humans remembered hidden gods as mystery; Khepra built entire courts around the terror of a name removed from existence. She does not kill in the open — she removes you from the record.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Amunet was born from the hidden half of divine power — the breath behind the name, the shadow behind the light. Where Aten-Ra is the sun that all can see, Amunet is the concealment that makes the sun possible. She is not darkness; she is the principle of hiddenness itself. Ancient humans glimpsed her through the Mythos Gate and remembered her as Amunet, the invisible one, consort of the hidden god Amun. But they saw only mystery. Amunet is not mysterious — she is the terror of a name removed from existence.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Aten Ra, Amunet is the one even the other deities forget exists. She is not absent — she is concealed, and concealment is her nature, not her choice. Aten-Ra's radiance needs her shadow to have depth. Khemet's dawn needs her night to have meaning. She is the hidden breath that gives the visible power its weight. The faction uses her for what no other deity can do: removing threats that cannot be fought openly. She does not kill; she erases.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Amunet by making her visible. When the Hollow leaked through the threshold, it stripped concealment from everything it touched — including her. For the first time, Amunet was seen, and being seen was not just uncomfortable; it was existential damage. Her hidden breath heart, which had always pulsed in shadow, began beating in light, and every pulse revealed what she had spent eternity concealing. The wound taught her that visibility is not truth — it is vulnerability.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In The First Reopening, Amunet is the assassin who moves through the shadow the Hollow creates. Paradoxically, the Hollow's erasure gives her more concealment to work with — the absence of things becomes her camouflage. Her shadow-veil was-sceptre phases between visible and invisible, and her name-erasure verdict removes enemies from the tactical record. The campaign tests whether erasure is the ultimate power or the ultimate fear — and whether being forgotten is worse than being destroyed.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Amunet's flaw is that she cannot be known without being diminished. Her power IS her concealment. Every time she reveals herself, she loses part of what makes her divine. The Hollow, which strips concealment from everything, is her exact opposite — and her exact mirror. Both erase; both are defined by absence. Her conflict: is the hidden name more powerful than the spoken one, or is concealment just another word for fear? The terror of a name removed from existence may be the terror of a being who removes her own name first.

chapters.shortBackstory: Nikos is war fury and victory personified — the Ares-Nike-source who proves that glory requires chaos and that victory without passion is just arithmetic.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Nikos was born from the bloodlust that makes victory possible. He is the disruptor who breaks enemy order by embodying chaos that precedes triumph. Ancient humans split his nature across Ares and Nike — but Nikos is both: the fury and the win.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Olympian, Nikos produces results others cannot. His star-lance disrupts through sheer aggressive force. He is not loved; he is needed. Glory requires the very chaos that threatens order.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Nikos by giving him victory without meaning. The Hollow removed enemies so completely there was nothing to defeat. Fury requires a target, and the Hollow removes both.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In the Laurel Senate Trials, Nikos breaks the trial's careful structure and forces glory to prove itself through real combat. His star-lance channels war fury into targeted disruption. But the Hollow cannot be defeated because it was never there.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Nikos's flaw is that he equates fury with courage and calm with cowardice. The Hollow teaches him that fury against absence is not courage — it is just noise. His conflict: is the warrior who only values passion wise, or is his fury a limitation mistaken for a virtue?

chapters.title: Personal Conflict

chapters.shortBackstory: Kageyori is the shadow-gate disruptor — the Oni-source whose necessary transgression keeps shrine law from becoming a cage.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Kageyori was born from the taboo broken — the transgression when sacred law becomes so rigid it prevents the sacred from functioning. He is the disruptor who breaks shrine law when shrine law breaks the shrine. Ancient humans saw him as the Oni — but they saw the demon and missed the necessity.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Kami, Kageyori breaks what needs breaking when no one else will. His shadow-gate disruption severs enemy coordination. He is not loved; he is needed — the Oni at the gate who does the violence the sacred cannot do to itself.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Kageyori by making his transgression meaningless. The Hollow removes the laws he was meant to break — there is nothing to transgress. Taboo requires law to exist.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In the Kami Mirror Tempest, Kageyori breaks corrupted shrine defenses. His iron-club sceptre channels taboo-force into disruption. But the Hollow has already removed the laws worth breaking.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Kageyori's flaw is that he equates transgression with truth. If a law is breakable, it was false. But the Hollow removes laws not because they were false but because they were erased. Transgression against emptiness is not truth — it is just violence.

chapters.shortBackstory: Hanae is the blossom-ward sustain — the Ryujin-source whose water-sovereignty heals through flow. She washes away what cannot be saved and nourishes what remains.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Hanae was born from the sea-palace — the deep water that heals by washing away what cannot be saved and nourishing what remains. She is the sustain who restores through flow. Ancient humans saw her as Ryujin — but they saw the dragon and missed the mercy.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Kami, Hanae is the reason the faction can lose and continue. Her blossom-ward washes away damage and nourishes what survives. She fights for continuation, not preservation.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Hanae by making her water flow toward nothing. The Hollow's erasure created spaces where healing water vanished. Flow requires a destination, and the Hollow removes destinations.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In the Kami Mirror Tempest, Hanae washes corruption from the battlefield and nourishes allies. But some wounds are not wounds — they are absences, and water cannot heal what was never injured.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Hanae's flaw is that she accepts loss too easily. Her water-nature means she washes away what cannot be saved without fighting to save it. The Hollow teaches her that some things should be fought for even when the odds say otherwise.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Kami, Onimaru strikes with combined authority of the Sacred Kingdoms' most powerful symbols. His triple-authority strike handles targets that cannot be defeated by single-force Deities.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Onimaru by separating his three treasures. The Hollow severed the connection between mirror, sword, and jewel — his unified strike became three separate, weaker attacks.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In the Kami Mirror Tempest, Onimaru provides long-range bombardment through the combined regalia strike. But the Hollow disrupts the regalia's unity — his strikes come apart, each treasure hitting separately and weaker.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Onimaru's flaw is that he believes his power comes from the treasures, not from himself. Without the regalia, he feels like nothing. The Hollow teaches him that the treasures are expressions of his nature, not sources of it.

chapters.title: Gate Wound

chapters.title: Campaign Role

chapters.shortBackstory: Yamabito is the stone-prayer assassin — the Yokai-source who exists in the twilight between existence and non-existence. He makes enemies uncertain whether they were ever alive.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Yamabito was born from the twilight — the boundary between what exists and what does not. He is the assassin who operates in ambiguity. Ancient humans saw the yokai — but they saw the haunting and missed the function. Yamabito exists in the gap the Hollow creates.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Kami, Yamabito handles what exists in the margins. His liminal nature perceives things between states — not quite real, not quite erased. The faction uses him to find what the Hollow has partially erased — things that can still be recovered if reached in time.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Yamabito by making his twilight permanent. The Hollow expanded the liminal space so large he could no longer find his way back to either side. Living in twilight is only bearable when dawn and dusk still exist.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In the Kami Mirror Tempest, Yamabito operates in the liminal gaps the Hollow creates. His stone-prayer sceptre phases between existence and absence, reaching partially-erased allies. But the expanding twilight means he is increasingly lost in the gap.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Yamabito's flaw is that he has never fully committed to existing. He is always half-present. The Hollow teaches him that the twilight is not a safe space — it is the edge of erasure, and living there too long makes you forget which side you started on.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Dagoran was born from the root-crown — the deep earth authority that says 'this ground is claimed, and the claim is living.' He is the defender whose power grows from the terrain itself. Ancient humans saw him as the Dagda — but they saw the abundance and missed the sovereignty.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Tuatha, Dagoran is the ground. His root-crown authority makes the terrain itself a member of the faction. He does not stand at the front line; he IS the front line, because the front line is the earth.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Dagoran by killing his roots. The Hollow removed patches of earth — un-creating them. His root-crown found gaps where roots simply stopped, leading to nothing.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Roots Below the Gate, Dagoran's root-crown creates living terrain that fights for the faction. His root-iron shield staff grows defensive walls from the earth. But the Hollow creates dead earth — patches where roots find nothing.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Dagoran's flaw is that he treats everything as soil to be tended — including people. His care is genuine but also controlling. The Hollow teaches him that some things cannot be grown — they can only be protected while they grow themselves.

chapters.title: Campaign Role

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Melian's flaw is that she has never wanted to leave the otherworld. She finds the real world flat and dull. The Hollow teaches her that the real world, with all its imperfection, is worth fighting for — because the otherworld only exists as a reflection of it.

chapters.title: Faction Bond

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Nimue by making her inspiration meaningless. The Hollow removes targets so completely there is nothing to inspire. Her flame ignites emptiness, and emptiness does not burn.

chapters.title: Campaign Role

chapters.title: Origin

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Cernan by making his mastery meaningless. The Hollow removed the skills he used — warriors who had mastered a technique were erased, and the technique went with them. Adaptability requires options, and the Hollow removes options.

chapters.title: Campaign Role

chapters.title: Personal Conflict

chapters.text: Nyxara was born from the descent — the geography of punishment grown from the weight of every sin. She is the controller who shapes the battlefield through prison geography. Ancient humans saw Hell — but they saw the punishment and missed the architecture. Confinement is control.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Nyxara makes the battlefield a prison. Her flameborn-court reshapes terrain into confinement — corridors that close, pits that open, walls that rise. She works with Varkul — he sentences, and she builds the prison the sentence requires.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Nyxara by making her prisons empty. The Hollow removes the imprisoned — and a prison with no prisoners is not architecture; it is just empty corridors.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Nyxara creates terrain that traps and confines enemies. Her flameborn-court staff makes the battlefield a sentence. But empty prisons are not control; they are just architecture.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Nyxara's flaw is that she has never seen a prison she wanted to open. Confinement is her answer to everything. The Hollow teaches her that some prisons should be opened, and the controller who never opens a door may have trapped her own faction inside her need to confine.

chapters.title: Divine Origin
chapters.text: Asmodeus is not a mortal hero inspired by myth. Asmodeus is the actual god recognized by Infernal Dominion source culture, born from the supernatural laws of The Infernal Dominion. Their domain — burning desire, infernal appetite, temptation, and destructive passion — determines their symbols, weapons, posture, combat instincts, and relationship to sacred authority.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Within Infernal Dominion, Asmodeus expresses the civilization rather than merely representing it. Their visual identity must carry the materials, beauty standards, divine symbols, and sacred rules of The Infernal Dominion. Their gameplay role, Breaker, must grow from mythology first and mechanics second.

chapters.title: Mythos Gate Wound
chapters.text: During the Ascension era, Asmodeus can interact with The Black-Iron Gate because divine beings are intrinsically connected to their Realms. The Gate does not become a simple teleportation portal; it is a mysterious boundary where separate mythological realities become traversable. Asmodeus understands some rites of crossing, but not the complete origin of the Mythos Gates.

chapters.title: Dungeon Role
chapters.text: When selected by the player, Asmodeus enters the dungeon alone as one god or goddess against multiple enemies. No army follows. No squad shares control. Every room, trap, shrine, relic, elite, and boss encounter must test how burning desire, infernal appetite, temptation, and destructive passion survives pressure from creatures, rival Realm laws, and unstable Gate conditions.

chapters.title: Ascension Conflict
chapters.text: Ascension is the current story arc, not the permanent end-state of the Mythos Gates universe. For Asmodeus, Ascension means restoration, awakening, evolution, or expansion of existing divine power. Their personal conflict is to recover strength without reducing Infernal Dominion mythology into raw fuel for the crisis.

chapters.shortBackstory: Azrakar is the chainwarden breaker — the Devils-source whose court violence shatters what resists Infernal authority. The chaining is the breaking.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Azrakar was born from the court — where power is not earned but taken. He is the breaker who shatters resistance through court-sanctioned violence. Ancient humans saw devils — but they saw the hierarchy and missed the violence. Azrakar's chains do not just bind; they break.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Azrakar ensures resistance is temporary. His chainwarden breaking shatters any defense that stands against Infernal authority. The breaking is always sanctioned by the court, which means it is always legal.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Azrakar by making his chains wrap nothing. The Hollow removes what he was chaining — and chains that wrap emptiness are not restraints; they are just metal loops.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Azrakar shatters enemy defenses through court-sanctioned violence. His chainwarden flail channels Infernal authority. But the Hollow removes the resistance — there is nothing to chain.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Azrakar's flaw is that he has never encountered resistance he respected. All resistance is defiance, and all defiance is crime. The Hollow teaches him that some resistance is not defiance — it is survival.

chapters.shortBackstory: Orryx is the ash-dominion disruptor — the Contracts-source whose Faustian bargains disrupt enemy order through debt. The terms are always worse than combat.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Orryx was born from the bargain — when one being offers another something they need at a price they cannot afford. He is the disruptor who breaks through contracts. Ancient humans saw Faustian bargains — but they saw the temptation and missed the disruption. Orryx's contracts are weapons, and the signature is the surrender.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Orryx wins without fighting. His contract-disruption offers enemies terms worse than combat. He works with Varkul — Varkul creates consequences, and Orryx offers the contracts that make consequences seem like the better option.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Orryx by making his contracts meaningless. The Hollow removes the parties — and a contract with no parties is not a bargain; it is just paper.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Orryx breaks enemy coordination through contract-disruption. His ash-dominion staff offers Faustian terms that fracture alliances. But the Hollow removes the parties to the contract — there is no one to sign.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Orryx's flaw is that he has never made a contract he considered unfair. His Faustian nature means every deal is a valid exchange. The Hollow teaches him that some agreements are made under duress so extreme that consent is meaningless.

chapters.shortBackstory: Malvera is the ember-throne sustain — the Goetia-source whose grimoire-seals sustain through constrained power. She binds raw force into usable form.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Malvera was born from the seal — the sacred constraint that binds power into usable form. She is the sustain who restores by binding raw force into functional energy. Ancient humans saw the Goetia and grimoires — but they saw the seals and missed the sustenance. The conversion of chaos into order is the most reliable form of sustain.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Malvera is the reason the faction can use its own power safely. Her ember-throne binds raw Infernal force into usable energy, preventing the faction's power from destroying its wielders.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Malvera by making her seals unbindable. The Hollow removes the things her seals were constraining — and a seal with nothing to seal is not a constraint; it is just a symbol.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Malvera restores allies by binding raw battlefield energy into usable form. Her ember-throne staff creates grimoire-seals. But the Hollow removes the energy she would bind — there is nothing to seal.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Malvera's flaw is that she has never released a seal. Her Goetia-nature means everything must be bound. She has sealed things that should have been free. The Hollow teaches her that some things are stronger unsealed.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Kharon was born from the chain — the restraint that is also a weapon. He is the artillery who bombards with chains that bind at the moment of impact. Ancient humans saw Charon and the chains of Hell — but they saw the ferryman and missed the bombardment. Kharon chains the living, and the chaining is the sentence.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Kharon makes distance irrelevant through restraint. His chain-artillery strikes from the horizon, and each impact binds the target. He works with Nyxara — she builds the cells, and Kharon chains the targets into them.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Kharon by making his chains strike nothing. The Hollow removes targets — and chains that strike emptiness wrap around air.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Kharon provides ranged restraint through chain-bombardment. His black-iron staff launches chains that bind enemies at impact. But the Hollow removes targets before the chains arrive.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Kharon's flaw is that he has never seen a chain he wanted to break. His chains-nature means everything is better bound. The Hollow teaches him that some things are stronger unchained.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Sablex was born from the furnace — the industrial fire that is not warmth but process. He is the guardian who defends through hellfire so intense that approaching him is itself a punishment. Ancient humans saw hellfire — but they saw the fire and missed the industry. Sablex's furnace is a factory, and the product is defense through thermal consequence.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Sablex makes approaching the faction physically costly. His cinder-duke guardian creates a furnace-aura that damages everything that enters his zone. He works with Mordrath — Mordrath creates the border, and Sablex makes the border a furnace.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Sablex by making his furnace burn nothing. The Hollow removes the fuel — and a furnace with no fuel is not a fire; it is just a hot room.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Sablex creates furnace-zones that damage enemies who approach. His cinder-duke maul channels hellfire into a defensive aura. But the Hollow means some enemies have no bodies to burn.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Sablex's flaw is that he has never turned down the heat. Everything is always at maximum temperature. The Hollow teaches him that a furnace that never cools is not a defense; it is a barrier that isolates.

chapters.name: Zerath
chapters.shortBackstory: Zerath is the wound-gate assassin — the Horns-source who removes enemies through wounds that do not heal. The wound is a door that the Hollow can enter through.

chapters.title: Origin
chapters.text: Zerath was born from the wound that does not close — the injury that becomes a door. He is the assassin who opens wounds that the Hollow can enter through. Ancient humans saw horned demons — but they saw the horns and missed the function. A being with a wound that will not close is a being the Hollow can reach.

chapters.title: Faction Bond
chapters.text: Among the Infernal Dominion, Zerath makes the Hollow useful. His wound-gate opens enemies to Hollow influence. He is the faction's darkest tool: the one who weaponizes the enemy's erasure.

chapters.title: Gate Wound
chapters.text: The Mythos Gate wounded Zerath by making his wounds meaningless. The Hollow no longer needs his help — it has learned to erase without doors. The assassin who opened doors for the enemy may have taught the enemy to enter without them.

chapters.title: Campaign Role
chapters.text: In Cinders of Dominion, Zerath opens wounds that create vulnerabilities in enemy defenses. His wound-gate daggers create injuries that do not heal. But the Hollow has become independent of his wounds — it no longer needs doors.

chapters.title: Personal Conflict
chapters.text: Zerath's flaw is that he has never questioned whether opening doors for the Hollow makes him complicit in erasure. The being who taught the enemy how to erase without permission may be the being who created the problem he was designed to solve.
